issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Marcus Volkov: A Case of Combat-Related PTSD

Marcus Volkov was forty-nine when he finally made the appointment, though his wife Elena had been urging him to do so for months. He was a city council member representing the third ward—a position he had held for six years with the kind of steady competence that came from his earlier career as a structural engineer. That steadiness, however, had become increasingly difficult to maintain. The traumatic event that now governed his life had occurred fourteen years earlier, during his second deployment to Afghanistan as a reserve officer. An IED had detonated near his vehicle during a supply convoy. Two soldiers in the vehicle ahead of his were killed; his own vehicle sustained heavy damage. Marcus himself was thrown against the interior wall, suffered a fractured collarbone, and spent the next several minutes certain he was going to die—trapped in the acrid smoke, unable to move his right arm, listening to screaming he could not locate.

In the years immediately following his return home, Marcus had managed to function adequately. He returned to his engineering firm, married Elena, and eventually transitioned into public service. But over the past three years, something had shifted. The symptoms that had always lurked beneath the surface began to metastasize into his daily life in ways he could no longer contain.

Sleep had become nearly impossible. He would lie beside Elena in the dark, his mind racing through fragmentary images—the smell of burning metal, a soldier's face he could not quite place, the sensation of being unable to breathe. The images came without narrative coherence; they were shards rather than a story. When he tried to describe to Elena what had happened that day, he found himself losing the thread midway through, unable to reconstruct the sequence or explain why certain details mattered so much to him. He knew intellectually that the event was over, that he was home and safe, yet his body refused to accept this truth. His heart would race at unexpected sounds. His muscles would tense without warning. He had come to believe, with a certainty that no amount of reassurance could shake, that his own body was betraying him—that it was locked in a state of danger that his conscious mind could not override or escape.

The hypervigilance that had once served him in a combat zone now exhausted him in the council chambers. During meetings, he found himself monitoring the room obsessively: exits, positioning of other people, potential threats. He was equally vigilant about his own mind. He caught himself constantly scanning his thoughts, watching for signs that he was losing his grip on reality. The effort of this internal monitoring, combined with the impossibility of ever feeling truly safe, wore him down in ways that were becoming visible to others.

To manage the anxiety, Marcus had developed a pattern of sensory distraction. He kept the television or music running almost constantly—loud enough to drown out his own thoughts, to occupy the space where fear would otherwise settle. When he was in his car between meetings, he blasted talk radio. At home, there was always something playing. Elena had stopped commenting on it, though he could see the weariness in her eyes.

The most visible change, however, was his withdrawal from physical contact. Elena's touch, once welcome, had become intolerable. When she reached for his hand or tried to embrace him, his entire nervous system would revolt. He would startle violently if she touched him unexpectedly, his body flooding with alarm before his mind could catch up. He had begun to avoid situations where physical contact might occur—he no longer attended social gatherings where hugs were customary, and he had made excuses to stop attending his nephew's soccer games, where he might be slapped on the back or embraced. His marriage, which had been a source of stability, was beginning to show strain under the weight of his emotional distance and his body's rejection of the one person who loved him most.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment of clarity that frightened him more than the symptoms themselves. During a council session three weeks ago, a colleague had unexpectedly placed a hand on his shoulder in congratulation. Marcus had jumped so violently that he had knocked over his water glass, and the entire room had fallen silent. Afterward, in the parking garage, he had sat in his car and acknowledged something he had been avoiding: he could not keep living this way. His world had become unbearably small and unsafe, and he was running out of places to hide.
